titre: The new star of 1572: no parallax, so beyond the Moon
accroche: In 1572, Tycho Brahe measures a star that has appeared in Cassiopeia. It does not shift: it is farther than the Moon, and Aristotle's sky changes.
contenu_vulgarise:
For Aristotle, the world divides in two. Below the Moon, everything changes: winds, meteors, comets, which were then held to be exhalations of the atmosphere. Above, in the region of the stars, nothing is born and nothing dies. The heavens are perfect because they are immutable.

On November 11, 1572, Tycho Brahe, observing from Herrevad Abbey, in Scania, notices in the constellation Cassiopeia a very bright star that he had never seen there. It is already more brilliant than Jupiter. Around November 16 it will reach a magnitude of about −4, close to that of Venus, and it will remain visible to the naked eye until early 1574.

## What parallax makes it possible to settle

Tycho is not the only one to see it, and others, such as the Spaniard Jerónimo Muñoz, are also interested in its distance. Tycho is one of the most precise observers of the object, and he measures it. He has a simple principle to work with. A nearby object, like the Moon, shifts slightly against the background of the sky depending on where you view it from, or on the hour of the night, since the Earth's rotation carries us along. This shift, parallax, is greater the closer the object is.

Tycho compares the position of the new star with that of neighboring stars, at different hours. Nothing moves. The object shows no detectable diurnal parallax, and does not change position relative to the fixed stars. So it is farther than the Moon, and even among the stars.

He publishes his measurements in 1573 in *De nova stella*. To skeptics who place the object within the terrestrial sphere, he replies with vehemence in that work, according to the APS.

## The result is an absence

The form of the proof deserves notice: it rests on what Tycho does not find. No measurable shift, and all of Aristotle's physics on the immutability of the heavens is damaged. An absence of motion did more damage than a spectacular discovery.

Two clarifications. The word “supernova” does not yet exist, and Tycho is not the first to see the object: other European observers describe it, and Muñoz also takes an interest in its distance. Tycho is regarded as one of the most precise among them. More than four centuries later, study of the object showed it to be a type Ia supernova, that is, the explosion of a white dwarf that had accumulated too much matter taken from a companion star.

The sky of 1572 was not proved changeable by a theory. It was proved by an instrument, a clear night, and an astronomer who checked before concluding.

What remains of our oldest certainties when someone takes the trouble to measure?

repere.texte: On November 11, 1572, the star in Cassiopeia is already brighter than Jupiter. Around November 16, its magnitude reaches about −4; it will remain visible to the naked eye until early 1574, before being identified as a type Ia supernova.

carte.punch: A star appears in 1572. Tycho measures it: it lies beyond the Moon, and the sky changes.
carte.idee: Tycho Brahe compares the star in Cassiopeia with its neighbors and finds no parallax. It is therefore more distant than the Moon, which contradicts Aristotle. His proof is an absence of shift.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: In English, open access; an account of the observation and its significance.

quiz.question: Why does the absence of parallax prove that the 1572 star is distant?
choix: Because a nearby object, like the Moon, shifts against the background of the sky when you change your point of view
Because a very bright star is necessarily very distant
Because the stars neighboring Cassiopeia are the faintest in the sky
Because parallax can only be measured for very distant stars
quiz.explication: A nearby object shows a shift that is greater the closer it is: the Moon shows one. No detected shift means the object is much farther away. Brightness alone says nothing about distance.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Tycho's discovery contradict in Aristotelian cosmology?
choix: The idea that the Moon is made of celestial matter
The idea that comets come from the atmosphere
The idea that the planets revolve around the Earth
The idea that the region of the stars never changes
quiz_supplementaire.explication: For Aristotle, change exists only below the Moon and the region of the stars is immutable. A new star beyond the Moon contradicts that point. The other ideas were not called into question by this measurement.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the identification of this object turn out to be, centuries later?
choix: A variable star pulsing like a Cepheid
A type Ia supernova, the explosion of a white dwarf
A collision between two neutron stars
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Study of the object led to its classification as a type Ia supernova, the explosion of a white dwarf that had accumulated matter. It is neither a comet, nor a Cepheid, nor a merger of neutron stars.
